newsitem.title: USA: U.S. medical device firms' Q2 growth seen solid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. medical device firms' Q2 growth seen solid.

text.p: Most major U.S. medical device manufacturers are expected to report another quarter of solid earnings gains, despite continued pressures on top-line growth from currencies and flat pricing trends.
Based on First Call estimates, profit increases will run about 13 percent over coming weeks as large makers of heart valves, pacemakers and such report second-quarter results.
"These companies are able to develop good sales growth and maintain very strong margins, even in this new managed care environment," said Montgomery Securities medical technology analyst Kurt Kruger.

Reflecting their success, eight of nine large-cap medical device stocks were trading at or near two-year highs Friday, riding a year-old flight to quality in the sector. Meanwhile, formerly hot small-caps -- like Heartport Inc and CardioThoracic Systems Inc -- flirted with new lows.

"If this is a real bull market, it's going to come back and pick up the mid- and small-cap names that it's left behind in the last year or so ... I believe this is going to happen," said Piper Jaffray medical technology analyst Arch Smith.
On the technology front, analysts said to look for a burst of new activity in the second half of the year as new stents and implantable defibrillators begin to emerge.
"We're in between a product cycle here now," said Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Discover analyst Glenn Reicin. "It gets better in the second half with new product introductions."

In spite of rapid growth in key markets, sales expansion among large-cap firms is being tempered by currency translations. In a preview of full results expected later this month, Boston Scientific Corp said July 7 its quarterly revenues would grow 25 percent year-over-year, but would have grown 28 percent if not for currencies.

Other sector leaders heavily dependent on exports, such as Medtronic Inc and Guidant Corp, can be expected to absorb similar hits. "Currencies continue to take their toll in the quarter," Reicin said.

Finally, managed healthcare firms continue to demand and receive big discounts, preventing device firms from pushing through price increases. "You're seeing zero price increases and some price decreases," said Wasserstein Perella medical technology analyst Robert Dunne.
If the biggest impact of both these factors is to cut a percentage point or two off double-digit growth rates, however, analysts said the industry is in good shape.
"These companies are just driving economies off of larger volumes and it's working like a charm for them," Kruger said.
